boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Glasgow record (October 15, 1864) in Price's Missouri Expedition [September-October 1864]. The same-day capture of Sedalia, the surrenders of Paris and Carrollton and Price's recruiting at Boonville are context. The NPS detail page for MO022 is an empty template, so the frozen Arnold row and its description stand for the NPS/CWSAC family. Campaign-wide marches, recruiting, destruction, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Garrison (800) and unknown, with a side strength of 800 for the Union garrison. Price says he sent Clark with his own brigade and 500 of Jackman's brigade across the river, with Shelby and part of his division and a section of artillery on the west bank, and that between 800 and 900 prisoners were taken. Britton gives the estimate of Captain Kirkham and other Federal officers that Clark had 5,000 to 7,000 men on the field, and says Harding's troops including militia did not exceed 750.
claims.rationale: An imported bound, unit identifications, a prisoner count and a participant estimate; no return for either side. None is adopted as a matched opening strength.

claims.value: Britton says the militia had thrown up breastworks around a square on a high point in town, adequate against an enemy without artillery, that the Missouri turns south at Glasgow, and that Shelby's battery fired from a sand bar across the river while Clark invested the town on the south, east and north. The frozen description names the fortifications on Hereford Hill.
claims.rationale: Ground described by a history and a summary; no map verification.

claims.value: Price says he was told some 5,000 arms were stored in the City Hall, which was burned with the arms before the surrender, and that the captures included about 1,200 small-arms, as many overcoats, 150 horses and a steamboat. Britton says the defenders' ammunition was nearly exhausted when terms were agreed.
claims.rationale: A depot report, captures and one statement on ammunition; no supply return.

claims.value: Price ordered Clark to cross at Arrow Rock and capture the place at daylight, with Shelby diverting attention from the west bank. Britton says Harding believed his troops and militia behind rifle-pits and brick houses could hold against the guerrilla forces he expected. The frozen description says the detachment was sent to liberate weapons and supplies.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from an interested report, a history and the frozen description.

claims.value: Price says Clark could not begin his attack until an hour after Shelby had engaged. Britton says Harding refused two demands to surrender and accepted terms at the third; the frozen description says Harding surrendered around 1:30 pm. The frozen commanders are Brigadier Generals John B. Clark and Joseph Shelby and Colonel Chester Harding.
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report, a history and the frozen description; no automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 450 total (US 400; CS 50). Britton gives Harding's report of 11 killed (read 1 1 in OCR) and 32 wounded and Colonel Colton Greene's of 7 killed and 46 wounded in his brigade, with Jackman's loss unreported. Price gives 800 to 900 prisoners and calls his own loss comparatively small.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap.

open_questions: Harding's report (No. 48) and the Glasgow subordinate reports, Clark's, Greene's and Shelby's reports, and Kirkham's account cited by Britton remain deferred.

Rosecrans's, Pleasonton's and Curtis's reports, the subordinate Union and Confederate reports in Volume XLI Part 1, the organization of Price's army (No. 89), Maclean's itinerary (No. 90), the Price Court of Inquiry, Hinton's 1865 Rebel Invasion of Missouri and Kansas, maps and returns remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC is one family (the NPS battle page plus the frozen Arnold rows). Wiley Britton's The Civil War on the Border, volume II (Putnam, 1899) is a retrospective history by a Union participant; by its preface the larger operations are based mainly on the published official reports, so it is not independent of the Price report family. Price's September 19 and November 2 dispatches and his December 28, 1864 report (Official Records Series I, Volume XLI, Part 1, No. 88) are one family of interested Confederate accounts. The Official Records volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
